title: Political Legitimacy
hook: Power can rest on fear alone, but it lasts when people believe it is rightful. That belief — legitimacy — is what separates authority from mere force.
key_points: Legitimacy is the widely shared belief that a government's right to rule is justified.
It turns naked power into authority people accept voluntarily, not just out of fear.
Max Weber identified three sources: tradition, charisma, and legal-rational rules.
In democracies, legitimacy rests mainly on lawful procedures and the consent expressed in elections.
content_html: A government can hold power through sheer force, but force is expensive and brittle — it requires constant coercion and invites resistance. Legitimacy is what makes power durable: it is the widely shared belief that a government's right to rule is justified, so that people obey because they accept its authority as rightful, not merely because they fear punishment. This belief is the difference between a regime that must watch its citizens and one that its citizens largely accept.
extra_html: The sociologist Max Weber offered the classic map of where legitimacy comes from, identifying three pure types. Traditional authority rests on long-established custom — "we have always been ruled this way," as with hereditary monarchs. Charismatic authority flows from devotion to an exceptional leader's personal qualities. Legal-rational authority, the dominant form in modern states, rests on impersonal rules and offices: people obey the law and the office, not the individual. Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that real governments usually blend these sources. In a democracy, legitimacy leans heavily on the legal-rational type — lawful procedures, constitutional limits, and the consent expressed through free elections — which is why disputed elections or rule-breaking by leaders can damage a government's standing even when it keeps physical control.

related.title: The Social Contract
related.hook: Why should anyone obey the state? The social contract answers: people trade some freedom for the security and order that only collective authority can provide.

related.title: What Government Is For
related.hook: Every society needs a way to make and enforce collective decisions — that shared system of authority is what we call government.

related.title: The Rule of Law
related.hook: The principle that everyone — including those in power — is bound by the same publicly known laws, applied equally.

flashcards.prompt: What distinguishes legitimate authority from mere force?

choices.text: People accept it as rightful, not only out of fear of punishment
It always controls a larger army
It never has to enforce any laws

flashcards.explanation_html: Force compels; legitimacy persuades. Authority is accepted as rightful, so compliance does not depend on constant coercion.

flashcards.prompt: Which three sources of legitimate authority did Max Weber identify?
flashcards.explanation_html: Weber's classic typology: legitimacy can rest on long-standing tradition, a leader's personal charisma, or impersonal legal-rational rules.
